_about: The shared vocabulary of the story database. validate.js reads this file; SCHEMA.md explains it. Add to it deliberately: every action, channel, fact and flag a storylet uses must be listed here.

categories.title: Routine and daily life
categories.theme: Commutes, regular meals, the same seat, errands, and the small variations and broken routines where story starts.

categories.title: Work and money
categories.theme: Shifts, a bad day, overtime, side gigs, debts, payday, and the job that ends or begins.

categories.title: Home and household
categories.theme: Cohabitants, chores, a lockout, a broken appliance, a landlord, and moving things in or out.

categories.title: Family
categories.theme: Siblings, parents visiting, a family dinner, a disagreement, looking after someone.

categories.title: Friendship
categories.theme: Regular meetups, a new friend, a favor, drifting apart, a falling out and making up.

categories.title: Romance and dating
categories.theme: A first date, a crush, a breakup, a partner others do not know about, an ex reappearing. Cozy, never explicit.

categories.title: Neighbors and community
categories.theme: Borrowing, a noise feud, carrying things for each other, a block gathering, the stall keeper who knows everyone.

categories.title: Secrets and misunderstandings
categories.theme: The ambiguity setups and their reveals. Each setup leaves at least two truths open and has a reveal for every one.

categories.title: Conflict and rivalry
categories.theme: Arguments, grudges, competition over a stall spot or a job, and the confrontation that never comes.

categories.title: Nightlife
categories.theme: The club, a bar regular, a night out going wrong, a turn away at the door, a late walk home.

categories.title: The street and the law
categories.theme: Muggings, lurkers and police seen from the edges: a victim afterward, a witness, someone avoiding the station, a lurker with a day job.

categories.title: Weather and the city
categories.theme: Rain changes plans, a metro delay, a long night, the city's moods.

categories.title: The player's city
categories.theme: Reactions to what the player builds, plus displacement and closures: homes demolished, workplaces removed, new people moving in.

categories.title: Milestones
categories.theme: A new job, moving out, a birthday, a farewell, someone new arriving.

categories.title: Quiet moments
categories.theme: Pure texture with no consequences: a plant, the rain, a stray, a long time on a bench.

pick-up.desc: pick up something dropped or left

shrug.desc: a shrug, a turn away, a shake of the head

seen.desc: an action the camera shows: entering a building with someone, carrying a box, waiting at a drop-off. Never carries names, relations, feelings or plans.

conversation.desc: overheard in person while watching either speaker. What the speaker says, as said.

phone.desc: a call: only the watched person's side is heard, so the other party and half the story stay unknown.

feed.desc: a public feed post read on the monitor. What they chose to say, sometimes vague or performative, never the whole truth.

document.desc: a delivery label, a nameplate on a door, a work uniform or badge, a notice, a ticket, a loyalty card. Verified.

introduction.desc: someone introduces them by name and relation. Verified for the relation as stated.

placeholders.{A}: the role's name for the log: 'Subject' until a name is learned, then the first name (or full name once verified)
placeholders.{A.desc}: a descriptor until named: 'an unknown female resident', 'a man in a courier jacket'; the name (with relation, if learned) afterward
placeholders.{A.first}: first name (only valid in reveal lines, where the name has just been learned)
placeholders.{A.full}: full name (only valid in reveal lines)
placeholders.{A.job} {A.employer} {A.home} {A.age}: job title, employer, home (as a place descriptor) and age range, only valid in reveal lines
placeholders.{A.rel}: the relation, as a word, of that role to A (for A: to B): "sister", "landlord". Only valid in reveal lines; a relation reveal teaches it
placeholders.{place}: the main place of the beat: 'the noodle stall', 'the north square'
placeholders.{n}: a count or a duration number
placeholders.{item}: a carried or handed thing: 'a box', 'a paper bag'
placeholders.{S}: hearsay only: the speaker (the watched person)
placeholders.{L}: hearsay only: the listener, as a descriptor
placeholders.{A.addr}: what the other person calls this role by relation: "Mom" or "Dad" for a parent, "Grandma" or "Grandpa" for a grandparent. Only valid in reveal lines; it states the relation
placeholders.{seen}: how many separate days the watcher has seen this person at this beat's place, counting today. Only in reveal lines; a line with it is skipped until the count is 2 or more

passing._about: Names in passing: a rule of the engine, not a storylet. When a watched beat has the subject and someone who knows them (any relation but a stranger) talking face to face, one of them may say the other's name. Each line teaches exactly the name it contains. Chances are per watched beat; the engine adds at most one passing line per storylet and never repeats a name already known.
toA: Overheard: {B.desc} says "{A.first}" and waits for {A} to look up.
Overheard: {B.desc} says: "Thanks, {A.first}. I owe you one."
Overheard: {B.desc} says: "{A.first}. Good to see you."
byA: Overheard: {A} says "{B.first}" twice before {B.desc} turns around.

phone._about: When a phone-call beat of the subject is watched, they may answer with their own name.
lines: Comm, one side: {A} answers: "{A.first} speaking."
Comm, one side: {A} says: "Yes, it's {A.first}. Who's this?"
Comm, one side: {A} says: "This is {A.first}. Go ahead."
Comm, one side: {A} says: "{A.first}. Yes. No, I can talk."

nameTag._about: Jobs with a counter or a uniform wear a name tag. When the subject is watched at one of the places listed for their job, the tag may be read. A document, so verified.
lines: Name tag on {A.his} apron: {A.first}.
Badge at {A.his} collar: {A.first}.
Stitched over the pocket: {A.first}.
A tag on {A.his} lanyard reads {A.first}.

orderCall._about: At a counter the keeper calls the order by name. Any queue-order or serve beat with the subject in it.
lines: Overheard: the keeper calls out: "{A.first}! Two skewers, extra chili."
Overheard: the keeper calls out: "Order for {A.first}!"
Overheard: the keeper reads the slip aloud: "{A.first}, one broth."
Overheard: the keeper asks a name for the order. {A} says: "{A.first}."

parcelLabel._about: A parcel left for the subject has a label. Not in storylets that already turn on a label (they have their own document reveal).
lines: Name on the parcel, upside down from here: {A.full}.
Delivery tag, face up on the step: {A.full}.
The address label on the box reads {A.full}.

doorPlate._about: A home with one resident has one name on the door plate. Seen when the subject comes or goes by the home door. Shared homes are left to the storylets (a plate with two names is a puzzle of its own).
lines: Plate by the door: {A.full}.
One name on the door plate: {A.full}.
Nameplate beside the frame: {A.full}.

greeting._about: Someone who knows the subject passes in the street and says hello by name. The engine picks the passerby from the subject's own people (a neighbor, a friend, a coworker, the keeper of a regular stall) who live or work nearby. Only on beats where the subject is out and about.
lines: {B.desc} passes {A} and lifts a hand: "{A.first}! Hey."
{B.desc} slows beside {A}: "{A.first}. Haven't seen you all week."
{B.desc} calls from across the street: "{A.first}! Later?" {A} waves back.
{B.desc} taps {A} on the shoulder in passing: "Hey, {A.first}."
{B.desc} nods at {A} on the way by: "{A.first}." {A} nods back.
{B.desc} stops long enough to say: "Rain later, {A.first}. Take a coat."

notInWorld._about: Things the city does not have, or wording the player must not be told. A line (even inside speech) that matches one of these is an error. The world has: residential tenements (laundry lines, potted plants, vines, lanterns, neon), shopfronts and food counters, luxury towers, factories; the Town Square (food stalls with trays, a steaming pot, skewers and buns; a koi pond; vending machines, kiosks, planters, trees, seats), lawns (picnics), the Market Plaza mall, the Sky Mall, the Cloud Pagoda hotel and spa, the Bath House (pools, front desk, tea counter), the Neon Dome club (queue, door staff, bar kiosk, snack stand), the Foundry, the Logistics Hub, the Hydroponic Farm, the Data Spire, the Radio station, the Police station (officers on patrol, police bikes), metro stations, platforms and trains, lifts with cabs, sky highways with traffic overhead, drones, delivery bots that wait at doors, rain and umbrellas, steam, holograms and ad screens, wanted posters, graffiti. People carry small things (bags, parcels, cups, bowls, a comm). There are no animals except the koi in the square's pond, and nobody feeds them.
